Where it began

Aaqib Javed was born in Sheikhupura, in Punjab, on 5 August 1972, and studied at Islamia College in Lahore. He was a right-arm fast-medium bowler who could move the ball both ways through the air, and he was very young when Pakistan picked him. His first Test came in 1989, while he was in his teens.

The player

He played 22 Tests between 1989 and 1998, taking 54 wickets at 34.70, with a best of 5 for 84. His bigger stage was one-day cricket, where he played 163 matches for Pakistan and was a member of the side that won the 1992 World Cup.

He saved some of his best days for India. On 25 October 1991 he took a hat-trick against them in a one-day international, aged 19 years and 81 days, which made him the youngest bowler to take one in that form of the game. Four of his six one-day player of the match awards came against India, and in 39 one-day games against them he took 54 wickets.

What made him special

Swing both ways and a cool head, at an age when most bowlers are learning their run-up. India's batsmen in particular saw rather more of him than they would have liked.

Batting was another matter. His 101 Test runs came at an average of 5.05, though a top score of 28 not out proves he could hang around when it counted. When a new generation of fast bowlers arrived in the late 1990s, his playing days ended at 26, early enough to leave room for a long second career.

Away from the middle

That second career was in coaching, and he was very good at it. He ran the coaching at Lahore's National Cricket Academy, and took Pakistan's under-19 side to the 2004 Under-19 World Cup title. He helped the young Afghanistan team find its feet, served as Pakistan's bowling coach, led the United Arab Emirates as head coach until 2016 and worked with Sri Lanka's fast bowlers.

From 2016 he spent eight years with the Lahore Qalandars, becoming head coach in December 2017. In October 2024 he joined Pakistan's selection committee, and late that year he took charge of the national men's team as interim head coach in every format. He backed an all-spin attack, a bold move in a country raised on fast bowling, and it brought a Test series win against England. People called it "Aaqib-ball".

And finally

He took exactly 54 wickets in Tests and exactly 54 in one-day games against India. Whether that was planning or coincidence, nobody has ever had the nerve to ask.
